library(shiny)
library(googleVis)
library(plotly)

shinyServer(function(input, output, session){
  output$userchoiceY <- renderUI({
    selectInput(inputId = "selecty", label="Select yvar", selected = "Pts", choices = names(TRIAL))

  })
  output$userchoiceX <- renderUI({
    selectInput(inputId = "selectx", label="Select xvar", selected = "Name", choices = names(TRIAL))

  })
  output$userchoiceName <- renderUI({
    selectInput(inputId = "selectN", label="Select Name", selected = "Nando De Colo",c(unique(as.character(TRIAL$Name))))

  })

  output$userchoiceYear <- renderUI({
    selectInput(inputId = "selectYe", label="Select Year", selected = "2001",c(unique(as.character(TRIAL$Year))))

  })

    selectInput(inputId = "selectT", label="Select Team", selected = "Fortitudo Bologna",c(unique(as.character(DatabaseEuroleague$Team))))

  output$p <- renderPlot({
  barplot(as.matrix(TRIAL[,input$userchoiceYe]*1000,main=input$userchoiceYe,ylab = input$selecty,xlab = input$selectN))

  })
  output$scat <- renderPlotly({
    ggplot(TRIAL[,colm()], aes(x=Pts, y=Min)) +
      geom_point(shape=1)      # Use hollow circles

    ggplotly()
  })

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I've deployed my app here so you can see the behavior: https://tcb-analytics.shinyapps.io/test

You can see on load the draft year is set to 2011, but then it changes to "" which causes an error in subsetting the data. I thought by simply setting selected = '2011' it would automatically display the data for that year on load.

Here's the code for server.R and ui.R.

server.R
library(shiny)

# Define server logic required to draw a histogram
shinyServer(function(input, output) {

  # Expression that generates a histogram. The expression is
  # wrapped in a call to renderPlot to indicate that:
  #
  #  1) It is "reactive" and therefore should re-execute automatically
  #     when inputs change
  #  2) Its output type is a plot

  dataInput <- reactive({
    players <- subset(players, draft_year == input$year)
    return(players)
  })

  output$distPlot <- renderPlot({
    players <- dataInput()
    weight <- players$weight # NFL Player Weight Data
    bins <- seq(min(weight), max(weight), length.out = input$bins + 1)

    # draw the histogram with the specified number of bins
    hist(weight, breaks = bins, col = 'darkgray', border = 'white')
  })
})

ui.R

library(shiny)

# Define UI for application that draws a histogram
shinyUI(fluidPage(

  # Application title
  titlePanel("Hello Shiny!"),

  # Sidebar with a slider input for the number of bins

messages.subject: Re: Hide rendered datatable
messages.subject_clean: Hide rendered datatable
messages.body_plain:
You can hide a datatable with `shinyjs::hide()`.

You can also use the ColVis extension of DT https://rstudio.github.io/DT/extensions.html

Or you could use the `visible` option to make certain columns not show https://datatables.net/reference/option/columns.visible

DT::datatable(mtcars,
                 options = list(
                 columnDefs = list(list(visible = FALSE,
                                          targets = 1:5))
                 )
   )

messages.body_plain:
Querybuilder passes what data are left after filtering back to DT to render. I think this works similar to the way DT filters with the basic column filters. Then based on what rows are displayed, I use input$table_all_rows to get what rows are being displayed by DT after filtering.

Meanwhile the DT is left hidden, for the most part (except for some basic information about how many items are in the table).

Hope this helps.

messages.subject: Re: object tag in an iframe tag in a shiny app can't find file in www/ directory
messages.subject_clean: object tag in an iframe tag in a shiny app can't find file in www/ directory
messages.body_plain: So I figured out the answer. Modern web browsers don't allow for a cross between http://localhost and file:/// when referencing files. Since Shiny runs on http://localhost, the use of file:/// was throwing everything off. In addition, when an iframe attempts to load a file, such as a PDF, the directory in which the html files that served as the source for the iframe is saved is the working directory. So the filepath for the PDF needs to account for that, either by having the file in the same folder, or using "../some.pdf" notation. Lastly, file names cannot have spaces in them. This was the biggest thing causing my file to not be found. In the end, the two fixes were this: 1) make sure the HTML files I generate dynamically for the iframes and any files I want to embed are saved in the same directory, and 2) standardize the file names. On Tuesday, December 1, 2015 at 3:41:45 PM UTC-5, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote: > So you're saying that users will run these Shiny apps on their own computers (i.e. running R on their own machines)? And you're trying to have the point directly to the file path on the hard drive? > > On Tue, Dec 1, 2015 at 12:33 PM Bryan Britten wrote: > > I've got an app that is trying to make a "localized" version of the JS Timeline that was developed by Northwestern University where localized means that data doesn't have to be sent to the cloud in order for timelineJS to use it. The app itself serves as an interactive builder for the timeline, which updates with each addition of an element. The full code is too much to post in this forum, but can be found here . > > > > My issue is this: In order to keep confidential information (files such as PDFs, sound files, images of suspects, etc) local, I do some behind the scenes checks about the files and if it needs to be local, I wrap it into an html file, which gets fed to the timeline, which gets wrapped in an iframe. When I try to do this with PDF documents, it coerces the HTML to include an iframe tag and it links the appropriate HTML file. The problem is that the nested file path, the one that links to the PDF document isn't being executed properly. It seems like no matter what I try, Shiny can't find the file. > > > > Here's the code that's relevant to this process: > > > > ``` > > file_name <- file.path(...) # this is what I need to fix, I think > > pdf_string <- paste('', sep = "") > > write(pdf_string, file = "www/some_pdf.html") > > ``` > > > > When the HTML renders, it comes out like this: > > > > ``` > > > > ``` > > > > Opening some_pdf.html outside of the shiny app works fine. So how do I leverage my file path inside of Shiny to get this to work? > > > > Thanks! > > > > -- > > You received this message because you are subscribed to the Google Groups "Shiny - Web Framework for R" group. > > To unsubscribe from this group and stop receiving emails from it, send an email to shiny-discus...@googlegroups.com. > > To view this discussion on the web visit https://groups.google.com/d/msgid/shiny-discuss/37627b99-b5c6-4757-8f90-eccb2770e093%40googlegroups.com . > > For more options, visit https://groups.google.com/d/optout.

Hi guys, I think I found where the problem is.
My app has some Chinese characters in it, and I think in some way that makes deployApps() unable to detect packages I used in this app.
I saved .R files with encoding in UTF-8. And I tried some apps with encoding in UTF-8 without Chinese characters in it.
And it's able to library the packages I need.
So I used helpers.R to library the packages I need, and source it in ui.R and server.R. And it worked! (helpers.R must not contain any Chinese characters)

Again, apology for my poor English. And a BIG thanks to Andy, thanks for your help!

Wish you guys have a nice day :)

For posterity purposes, I solved my problem by:
1) Disabling iptables in the guest VM
2) I changed the listening port from 3838 to Port 8080.

messages.subject: Using plot_click to create a vector, then send values of vector to C program
messages.subject_clean: Using plot_click to create a vector, then send values of vector to C program
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'll try to be clear about what I'd like to do.
I have a shiny app that displays a plot with what I'll call a base function (a semicircle) that does not change and a dynamic curve that is produced by a C program (a lagrangian interpolation program) that is called within the shiny app, which takes input parameters that are set using two slide bars.  One is an integer parameter ("anchors") indicating the number of anchor values (they are values that are randomly generated and lie on the semicircle; used to define the interpolation polynomial (lagrange polynomial), and the other is an integer parameter ("points") indicatign the number of values that are to be interpolated by the C program.
What I need to do is add functionality whereby clicking on the plot (created in ggplot) adds additional anchor values, and updates parameter values sent to the C program, resulting in an updated interpolation plot.
I'm thinking that using  plot_click to produce a vector of values that will be used in issuing a new call to the C program.  Only x coordinate values would be needed for the C program to run.  (The Y coordinates are calculated in the C program from the x coordinates.)

My functioning shiny app is as follows (it is a bit more complex than I described, as there are multiple base functions that can be
switched using a radio button.

Oh, another note: The "name" variable that is used in the C function call is sort of a hack whereby the exact character strings produced by the radio button are used in order to call the relevant C program.  There is one C program for each of the base functions.  I know there is a better way to do this so that I don't have to render the text for the exact names of the C functions, but I couldn't figure it out.

Thanks for any help with this.

library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)

argv_graphtest3 <- function (name, points, anchors)
{
  name2 = paste("/home/matto/education/STC/finalproject/", name, sep="")
  tempfilename = paste("/home/matto/education/STC/finalproject/", name, "temporary.txt", sep="")
  file.create(tempfilename)
  command = paste(name2, points, anchors, ">", tempfilename)
  system(command)
  data = read.table(tempfilename,header=FALSE)
  return (data)
}

semicircle <- function(x) (25-x^2)^.5
non_polynomial <- function(x) 6 + 10*(x-2) - 8*(x+1)^3 + x^5
non_linear <- function(x) 6 + 10*(x-.2) - 8*(x+.1)^3 + x^5
#test2 <- function(x) 6 + 4*x-(9.8/6)*x^2 + (1/6)*x^3
test4 <- function(x) 6 + 10*x - 8*x^3 + x^5

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Lagrange Interpolation"),
  sidebarLayout(
  sidebarPanel(
  sliderInput(inputId = "num",
              label = "Choose anchor points",
              value = 5, min = 1, max = 50),
  sliderInput(inputId = "num2",
              label = "Choose interpolated points",
              value = 50, min = 1, max = 500),
  radioButtons("basefunction", "select base function",
               list("degree_5_polynomial", "semicircle", "semicircle_unanchored", "degree_5_nonlinear"), "")
  ),
  mainPanel(
    plotOutput("hist"), width = "100%")
)
  )

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$hist <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(argv_graphtest3(input$basefunction, input$num2, input$num),
           aes(x=V2, y=V3)) + geom_point(shape = 1) + geom_line(colour = "black") +
      stat_function(fun = test4, colour = "green") +
      stat_function(fun = non_linear, colour = "blue") +
      stat_function(fun = semicircle, colour = "red") + ylim (-10, 20) +
      coord_fixed(1) + xlim(-10,10)

    #    hist(rnorm(input$num))
  }, height = 700, width = 600)
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

Hi,

What is the best way to render a regression table in shiny? I could generate a html table using stargazer

    set.seed(1272015)
    n<-1000
    x1 <- rnorm(n = n, mean = 7, sd = 2)
    x2 <- rnorm(n = n, mean = 4, sd = 2)
    treatment <- sample(x = c(1,0), size = n, replace = T, prob=c(0.3,0.7))
    y <- 2.1234*x1 + 1.1234*x2 + 0.5*treatment + rnorm(n, mean=0, sd=1)
    mydata = data.frame(x1, x2, treatment, y)
    lm1 <- lm(formula = y~x1+x2+treatment, data=mydata)

    stargazer::stargazer(lm1, type="html")

but, I'm not sure how to render it in shiny. For example:

    ## app.R ##
    library(shiny)
    library(shinydashboard)
    library(stargazer)

    ui <- dashboardPage(
      dashboardHeader(title = "Basic dashboard"),
      dashboardSidebar(),
      dashboardBody(
        # Boxes need to be put in a row (or column)
        fluidRow(
          box(title = "Regression table", renderUI(lm1))
        )
      )
    )

    server <- function(input, output) {

messages.subject: Re: Rendering MathML
messages.subject_clean: Rendering MathML
messages.body_plain:
This line:

return(withMathJax(output))

should be this instead:

return(withMathJax(HTML(output)))

The HTML() tells us that `output` is intended to be interpreted as raw markup, instead of text. We always have to assume text unless told otherwise, because while interpreting markup as text is broken and ugly, interpreting text as markup is often a difficult-to-detect security issue <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-site_scripting> which is much worse.

Even with HTML() in place, the output doesn't look right, but I'm afraid I'm not conversant enough in MathML to help.

It might be easier to debug if you compose your mathjax using functions instead of pasting strings together. This video will give you the background:

However, the MathML elements are not part of the Shiny tag vocabulary, so you'll have to create your own MathML functions:

math <- function(...) tag("math", list(...))
mtable <- function(...) tag("mtable", list(...))
mtr <- function(...) tag("mtr", list(...))

etc.

Then you can do things like:

math(
  mtable(
    lapply(data, function(x) {
      mtr(...)
    })
  )
)

You can call print() on such objects to see the generated markup at the R console.

messages.subject: How does shiny manage the state?
messages.subject_clean: How does shiny manage the state?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am new to R and shiny, both. I really like the way, shiny allows users to create the web UI's from R code. I was curious to know how R manages the state (reactive variables and other entities). The code for renderPlot shows a reference to "shinysession". Does this session hold cached values? I am just trying to understand shiny architecture better. In the eventReactive example available as part of the webinar, when the slider is moved, its current value is sent to the server and it then gets used later when the button is pressed. Where is the previous slider value stored?

What recommendations do shiny users have to write an application that supports fail over? Also, is there any way to debug a built-in shiny function like renderPlot?

Thanks
Sachin

messages.subject: Re: How does shiny manage the state?
messages.subject_clean: How does shiny manage the state?
messages.body_plain:
The eventReactive object caches its own value, effectively. The same is true of reactive(). The session object holds current copies of the user input but not too much else in terms of what's necessary for calculations. (I'm not sure how to shine light on how Shiny is implemented, it's quite a big topic and I'm still trying to figure out if knowing the implementation actually helps people write better apps.)

You can debug using debug(renderPlot), then running your app. It helps to install shiny with "R CMD INSTALL --with-keep.source shiny" (where shiny is the path to the shiny github project on your local disk).

For fail over you can use shiny server like any other webserver--put two or more behind a proxy or load balancer that supports fail over. If a server goes down you will lose existing sessions (due to the stateful nature of Shiny that's a bit tricky to solve) but future sessions will go to the new server.

-Jesse

messages.subject: Re: Load data before execution
messages.subject_clean: Load data before execution
messages.body_plain:
Look up the help file for & in R by typing ?`&`

The shorter one is vectorized which means it expects two vectors and it will show the result of "AND" between every pair of elements in the two vectors. The longer one has short-circuiting behaviour, which means it operates from left to right and the moment it runs into something that is FALSE, it will stop evaluating the rest of the arguments because if one of the args is false then we already know the whole statement is false.  It's a rather technical explanation, try Googling for "shortcircuit logical and"

messages.subject: Re: Rendering MathML
messages.subject_clean: Rendering MathML
messages.body_plain:
Changing the return statement to return(withMathJax(HTML(output))) did help but, as you noted, still left the rendered output looking strange.

After looking into the raw code a little more, I made a discovery that actually fixed everything (as far as I can tell). Within the raw code that I was pasting together, there were instances of something like this: <mtext><mrow><mtext>cbGroup1:cb3; cb4:</mtext></mrow></mtext>; in particular, <mrow><mtext> tags inside <mtext> tags. Once I removed the inner <mrow><mtext> tags (i.e., changed that example bit of code to <mtext>cbGroup1:cb3; cb4:</mtext>), Shiny rendered the output correctly.

It seems, then, the live demo on MathJax.org may be a little more tolerant/understanding of MathML than Shiny. All in all, however, my Shiny app is working well now and I'm quite happy it only took a relatively minor tweak of my code to get it to that point.

On Monday, December 7, 2015 at 2:55:45 PM UTC-7, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> This line:
>
> return(withMathJax(output))
>
> should be this instead:
>
> return(withMathJax(HTML(output)))
>
> The HTML() tells us that `output` is intended to be interpreted as raw markup, instead of text. >
> math <- function(...) tag("math", list(...))
> mtable <- function(...) tag("mtable", list(...))
> mtr <- function(...) tag("mtr", list(...))
>
> etc.
>
> Then you can do things like:
>
> math(
>   mtable(

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

Wanted to post a few concerns regarding a shiny app I had recently developed.

The main data fetches for the app are from an Aster database using the TeradataAsterR package and setting up RODBC drivers for the same. Other data pulls are 900mb worth of HTML files to be published as is on one of the tabs in the app.

The issues I have been facing are:

Important facts to note here:
 - The linux machine on which the app is hosted has 32gb RAM
 - Only 500mb of space is left on the drive on which the shiny app is defined

There are no other data connections or flat files being read.

Is there any way to optimize my app to not throw this error every few hours?

Also will using shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io> to host the app [paid version] result in more stable performance?

Thanks you!

messages.subject: Save shiny objects to an Rdata file
messages.subject_clean: Save shiny objects to an Rdata file
messages.body_plain:
I often wish that I could interactively work within my shiny application interactively, similar to using browse()in a function., and sometimes I use a shiny GUI to get to a state where I just want to save things.

So, I wrote something that can save all the shiny application objects,which uses Hadley's pryr package to recursively list the objects. So you need this somewhere (I think it belongs in global.R or server.R)
library(pryr)

In ui.R you need an action button.  You could add this to one of the existing shiny examples.
actionButton("save_objs", "Save Objects")

In server.R I have this code, which listens to save_objs:

    observeEvent(input$save_objs, {
        # Run whenever save_objs button is pressed

        print("** saving objects! **")

        ## Print the objects being saved
        print(rls())
        # ## Put  objects into current environment
        for(obj in unlist(rls())) {
            if(class(get(obj, pos =  -1))[1] == "reactive"){
                ## execute the reactive objects and put them in to this
                ## environment i.e. into the environment of this function
                assign(obj, value = eval(call(obj)))
            } else {
                ## grab the global variables and put them into this
                ## environment
                assign(obj, value = get(obj, pos =  -1))
            }
        }

        input_copy <- list()
        for(nm in names(input)){
            # assign(paste0("input_copy$", nm), value <- input[[nm]])
            input_copy[[nm]] <- input[[nm]]
        }

        ## save objects in current environment
        save(list = ls(), file = "shiny_env.Rdata", envir = environment())

        print("** done saving     **")
    })

I use print statements liberally during development, feel free to omit them.

This took me a while to figure out, so hopefully it will save someone else time (maybe even me later when I forget and google "R how to save objects in shiny").

As a side note, I can't understand how the rls can find the environment with the reactive objects.  It's not in my current budget to buy Hadley's Advanced Programming in R, so I'll have to wait to find out. I tried to get the objects directly with various combinations of parent.frame and parent.env, but I could only find Shiny internal objects and objects in my normal search path.  So... there's some clever stuff in that pryr package.

ui.r

library(shiny)

On Tuesday, 24 November 2015 00:33:24 UTC+5:30, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:

> We've made a simple but significant improvement to error handling in Shiny 0.12.2.9006. Errors now have stack traces!
>
> Adding stack traces touched a fair amount of low-level code in Shiny, so I'd greatly appreciate it if you could upgrade to the development version (devtools::install_github("rstudio/shiny")) and let me know if you see any problems. We're hoping to release to CRAN in the coming weeks.
>
> Consider this buggy app.R file:
>
> >  1: library(shiny)
> >  2: library(ggplot2)
> >  3:
> >  4: ui <- fluidPage(
> >  5:   plotOutput("plot")
> >  6: )
> >  7:
> >  8: server <- function(input, output, session) {
> >  9:   mydata <- reactive({
> > 10:     head(25, cars)
> > 11:   })
> > 12:
> > 13:   output$plot <- renderPlot({
> > 14:     ggplot(mydata(), aes(speed, dist)) + geom_point()
> > 15:   })
> > 16: }
> > 17:
> > 18: shinyApp(ui, server)
>
> Using the latest CRAN version of Shiny, running this app gives you output like this:
>
> > > shinyApp(ui, server)
> >
> > Listening on http://127.0.0.1:7416
> > Error : length(n) == 1L is not TRUE
>
> And that's it--no clue where the error originated.
>
> After installing the latest development version of Shiny the output becomes:
>
> > Listening on http://127.0.0.1:6212
> > Warning: Error in : length(n) == 1L is not TRUE
> > Stack trace (innermost first):
> >     96: stopifnot
> >     95: head.default
> >     94: head
> >     93: reactive mydata [~/app.R#10]
> >     82: mydata
> >     81: ggplot
> >     80: renderPlot [~/app.R#14]
> >     72: output$plot
> >      5: <Anonymous>
> >      4: do.call
> >      3: print.shiny.appobj
> >      2: print
> >      1: source
>
> The stack trace can be read from the bottom up: source() called print(), which called print.shiny.appobj(), which called do.call(), etc.
>
> Generally you'll want to scan from the top down and find the first (i.e. innermost, i.e. most recent) call that comes from your project files--in this case, frame 93 implicates line 10 of app.R, which has "head(25, cars)". Ah, we've reversed the order of the arguments, it should've been "head(cars, 25)".
>
> Notice that the numbers in the stack trace above aren't contiguous; it's missing entries for 6-71, 73-79, and 83-92. Shiny has a lot of internal plumbing, most of which is just not that interesting when you're trying to debug a problem in your app, so we try to hide uninteresting parts of the stack trace. If you suspect that useful information is being hidden, you can turn off the hiding with this option:
>
> > options(shiny.fullstacktrace = TRUE)
>
> Hope you find this change useful!
>
> -joe

messages.subject: RODBC Crashes Shiny Server
messages.subject_clean: RODBC Crashes Shiny Server
messages.body_plain:
So we've been struggling with this for a few days now and haven't made any progress on a solution. Below is the description of out problem:

We are running a Shiny Server (and Shiny Dashboard) on RedHat 6.7 (R version 3.2.2 Fire Safety) and have been running into a segfault when trying to query a database using RODBC. This happens when we source the file into app.R or make a query request to the database in the server.R file. When we run the same code in the R console it works just fine.

It seems like there must be some type of interaction between Shiny and RODBC that is causing this issue. As a workaround we are using the RJDBC, which works fine, but we're worried it isn't going to scale well for us. And it's quite slow.

Anyone have an idea what we can do to make RODBC work correctly?

If you would like more details you can see the SO post I made yesterday. I'm sorry to double posting but after searching far and wide we haven't found any helpful information.

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/34316243/rodbc-query-brings-down-shiny-server

Thanks!

-C

messages.subject: Shiny quickly shows the selected input but reverts back to first input
messages.subject_clean: Shiny quickly shows the selected input but reverts back to first input
messages.body_plain:
In this Shiny App, I am Uploading a .CSV file and then plotting different columns based on the channel chosen in a SelectInput

Everything is loading fine, but whenever I choose Time, Watts, Volts or Amps, the Dygraph chart quickly reverts back to graphing the Scan channel.  The Wattage, Voltage and Amp charts quickly show, but then it reverts back to the Scan input.  It does not stay on the channel that I choose.  It's almost as though it's going through a reactive loop and reverting back to the Scan (or whatever the first channel is).

Any ideas on how I can make it stop reverting back to the original channel and keep it on the Channel that I choose?

Here is a Sample Dataset that I am Loading <https://drive.google.com/file/d/0Bzg7bDcyZobbQ1RqTmpUSFVQMGM/view>

ui.R

    shinyUI(fluidPage(
      navbarPage("Engineering Data",
    tabPanel("Upload your Own File:",
                          sidebarLayout(
                            sidebarPanel(
                              fileInput('file1', 'Choose CSV File',
                                        accept=c('text/csv',
                                                 'text/comma-separated-values,text/plain',
                                                 '.csv')),
                              tags$hr(),
                              checkboxInput('header', 'Header', TRUE),
                              radioButtons('sep', 'Separator',
                                           c(Comma=',',
                                             Semicolon=';',
                                             Tab='\t'),
                                           ','),
                              radioButtons('quote', 'Quote',
                                           c(None='',
                                             'Double Quote'='"',
                                             'Single Quote'="'"),
                                           '"'),
                              selectInput("uploadChannels", label = "Choose Channel",
                                             choices = NULL)
                            ),
                            mainPanel(
                                  dygraphOutput('graph')
                            ))

                            )

                                   )))

server.R

output$graph <- renderDygraph({
        uploadedFile <- input$file1

        if (is.null(uploadedFile))
          return(NULL)

        # Clean up the loaded CSV File, convert Time column to a Time Object for Dygraph.
        uploadedFile <- read.csv(uploadedFile$datapath, header=input$header, sep=input$sep,
                                 quote=input$quote)
        uploadedFile$Time <- as.POSIXct(strptime(uploadedFile$Time,"%H:%M:%S"))
        uploadedFile$ctime <- strptime(paste(uploadedFile$Time), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")

        # Update the SelectInput and store the value in component5 to be used in the graph.

        observeEvent(uploadedFile, {
          updateSelectizeInput(session, 'uploadChannels', choices = names(uploadedFile))
        })
        selectedInput <- input$uploadChannels
        component5 <- uploadedFile[, selectedInput]

        xts(component5, uploadedFile$Time)  %>%
          dygraph()
         })

    })

Thanks.

Has anyone else been able to reproduce this issue?

messages.body_plain:
This chunk:

        observeEvent(uploadedFile, {
          updateSelectizeInput(session, 'uploadChannels', choices = names(uploadedFile))
        })

should be moved outside the output$graph <- renderDygraph({...}) section. You will also probably want to extract out the code that defines uploadedFile, and make that a reactive expression. So:

uploadedFile <- reactive({
  validate(need(input$file1, FALSE)) # This is like a better "if (is.null(input$file1)) return(NULL)"
  uf <- read.csv(input$file1$datapath
})

observeEvent(uploadedFile(), {
  updateSelectizeInput(session, 'uploadChannels', choices = names(uploadedFile()))
})

output$graph <- renderDygraph({
   # ... code that uses uploadedFile() ...
})

"sudo su - shiny" should put you into a shell as the shiny user, then you can launch R and try your code.

When I switch to the shiny user I can successfully run the queries. So that's good.

Would it make a difference if I've edited the shiny-server.conf file to run as my user name? Here is what my conf file looks like:

# Instruct Shiny Server to run applications as the user "shiny"
run_as usernam;

# Define a server that listens on port 3838
server {
  listen 3838;

  # Define a location at the base URL
  location / {
    app_dir /srv/shiny-server/rev_1;
    # Host the directory of Shiny Apps stored in this directory
    #site_dir /srv/shiny-server;

    # Log all Shiny output to files in this directory
    log_dir /var/log/shiny-server;

    # When a user visits the base URL rather than a particular application,
    # an index of the applications available in this directory will be shown.
    directory_index on;
  }
}

messages.body_plain:
Jonathan,

There are a variety of ways you can do this. First I want to point you to this article which gives general guide lines on how to manage libraries:

https://support.rstudio.com/hc/en-us/articles/215733837-Managing-libraries

For Shiny Server Pro you have the option to define r_path at granular levels. Please refer to this section of Admin Guide:

http://rstudio.github.io/shiny-server/latest/#r_path

You can also use exec_supervisor and pass in specific R library paths at different granular levels. Please refer to this section of Admin Guide:

http://rstudio.github.io/shiny-server/latest/#program-supervisors

And you also have the option to use packrat projects. An individual application could be a packrat project, tied to specific versions of all dependent packages, and deployed to Shiny Server Pro which will use those versions.

Hope this helps. Feel free to open support ticket if you are a Shiny Server Pro customer.

Best,
Fereshteh

With the bu

messages.subject: Re: Action button redraws current plot when changing input
messages.subject_clean: Action button redraws current plot when changing input
messages.body_plain:
The "if (is.null(fn3()) return(NULL)" is causing you to take a dependency on fn3.

You could remove that line and instead, after plotvalues <- evr(), check if plotvalues is null and return if so.

Better yet, remove all the checks for NULL, instead use validate/need (or with the upcoming Shiny release, you can use the new "req()" function to accomplish the same thing more concisely). Basically the way it works is, in fn1, if you're expecting input$foo to be non-NULL and you want to say "I can't continue" if that's not the case, you can do this:

fn1 <- reactive({
  validate(need(input$foo, FALSE))
  ... more code ...
})

The rest of your code should be the same except remove all the checks for NULL for fn1(), fn2(), etc. If fn1 executes while input$foo is NULL, then it and all its callers will abort silently. When input$foo is no longer NULL then the reactives will know to try again.

I also want to note that if "#plot stuff" makes calls to inputs, reactive values, or reactive expressions, then you'll want to wrap that in isolate({ ... }) as well to ensure that the action button is the only thing that can trigger plotting (well, that and resizing the browser window).

output$plot <- renderImage({
  plotvalues <- evr()
  isolate({
    ...
  })
})

However, if "plotvalues" is the only data you need, then you don't need to bother with the isolate.

messages.subject: Use gvisbarchart instead of barplot.
messages.subject_clean: Use gvisbarchart instead of barplot.
messages.body_plain:
I would like to know how could i create dynamic barcharts(googleVis) instead of those barplots in the code above.

#' @demo Archetypal basketball players based on player statistics;
#'   analysis from the manuscript "Archetypal athletes" by Eugster
#'   (2011)

library("SportsAnalytics")
library("archetypes")
library("RColorBrewer")
library("googleVis")
col_pal <- brewer.pal(7, "Set1")
col_black <- rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.2)

### Data: ############################################################

data("NBAPlayerStatistics0910")

dat <- subset(NBAPlayerStatistics0910,
              select = -c(Ejections, FlagrantFouls))

mat <- as.matrix(subset(dat, select = -c(League, Name, Team, Position)))

pcplot(mat, col = col_black, las = 2)

### Archetypes: ######################################################

set.seed(4321)
as <- stepArchetypes(mat, k = 1:10)

rss(as)
screeplot(as)

a4 <- bestModel(as[[4]])

### Archetypal basketball players:

parameters(a4)
barplot(a4, mat, percentiles = TRUE)

### Player interpretation: ###########################################

players <- function(which) {
  players <- list()
  players$which <- which
  players$mat <- mat[which, ]
  players$coef <- coef(a4, "alphas")[which, ]
  players$dat <- dat[which, ]

  players
}

### Archetypal players:

which <- apply(coef(a4, "alphas"), 2, which.max)
atypes <- players(which)

cbind(subset(atypes$dat, select = c(Name, Team, Position)),
      atypes$coef)

### Good players:

good_players <- function(atype, threshold) {
  which <- which(coef(a4, "alphas")[, atype] > threshold)

  good_coef <- coef(a4, "alphas")[which, ]
  good_dat <- subset(dat[which, ], select = c(Name, Team, Position))
  good_dat <- cbind(good_dat, good_coef)
  good_dat <- good_dat[order(-good_coef[, atype]), ]

  good_dat
}

good_threshold <- 0.95

players <- lapply(2:4, good_players, good_threshold)
players

messages.body_plain:
If you're visiting a server via IP, you can't just change the URL bar to display something else, not unless you actually redirect the browser to make a new request using the name instead of the IP. If you could just change the URL bar, then bad guys could trick you into visiting 1.2.3.4 and then change the URL bar to "bankofamerica.com <http://bankofamerica.com>".

You need to buy a domain name and not redirect it to the app, but actually configure the DNS server for that domain to point to the server IP address. This is called an "A record" and your domain host should have instructions for how to configure one.

For example:
https://www.godaddy.com/help/add-an-a-record-19238
http://wiki.dreamhost.com/Custom_DNS#A_record
https://www.namecheap.com/support/knowledgebase/article.aspx/319/78/how-can-i-setup-an-a-address-record-for-my-domain

> > 12:

>
> > Listening on http://127.0.0.1:6212
> > Warning: Error in : length(n) == 1L is not TRUE
> > Stack trace (innermost first):
> >     96: stopifnot
> >     95: head.default
> >     94: head
> >     93: reactive mydata [~/app.R#10]
> >     82: mydata
> >     81: ggplot
> >     80: renderPlot [~/app.R#14]
> >     72: output$plot
> >      5: <Anonymous>
> >      4: do.call
> >      3: print.shiny.appobj
> >      2: print
> >      1: source
>
> The stack trace can be read from the bottom up: source() called print(), which called print.shiny.appobj(), which called do.call(), etc.
>
> Generally you'll want to scan from the top down and find the first (i.e. innermost, i.e. most recent) call that comes from your project files--in this case, frame 93 implicates line 10 of app.R, which has "head(25, cars)". Ah, we've reversed the order of the arguments, it should've been "head(cars, 25)".
>
> Notice that the numbers in the stack trace above aren't contiguous; it's missing entries for 6-71, 73-79, and 83-92. Shiny has a lot of internal plumbing, most of which is just not that interesting when you're trying to debug a problem in your app, so we try to hide uninteresting parts of the stack trace. If you suspect that useful information is being hidden, you can turn off the hiding with this option:
>
> > options(shiny.fullstacktrace = TRUE)
>
> Hope you find this change useful!
>
> -joe

>   #  1) It is "reactive" and therefore should re-execute automatically

messages.body_plain:
I have code in many of my apps to load CSS files. I usually put them inside a `www/` directory and use

tags$head(tags$link(href = "style.css", rel = "stylesheet"))

I wanted to switch to using the `includeCSS()` function instead, but I noticed that it assumes the CSS file lives in the main app directory rather than inside `www/`.  Other resources such as images are also by default assumed to be under `www/` (I'm guessing this was done using `addResourcePath()?`), so I was just wondering if there was a reason this function doesn't make that same assumption?

messages.subject: Re: Is there a design reason why includeCSS() does not look inside www/ folder?
messages.subject_clean: Is there a design reason why includeCSS() does not look inside www/ folder?
messages.body_plain:
Why switch to includeCSS? The way you're doing it is how I would do it.

includeCSS takes an arbitrary file path, so there's no assumption at all about where it lives. It's simply resolving relative paths according to the current working directory. With images, you're probably talking about relative *URL* paths, and yes, those are mapped to www/ as the root directory. That's different because the path in question is sent to the client, and the client makes the request back to the server--hence the need to use www/ to make sure we don't serve up data that's not supposed to be public.

On Tue, Dec 29, 2015 at 6:17 PM Dean Attali <daat...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I have code in many of my apps to load CSS files. I usually put them inside a `www/` directory and use
>
> tags$head(tags$link(href = "style.css", rel = "stylesheet"))
>
> I wanted to switch to using the `includeCSS()` function instead, but I noticed that it assumes the CSS file lives in the main app directory rather than inside `www/`.  Other resources such as images are also by default assumed to be under `www/` (I'm guessing this was done using `addResourcePath()?`), so I was just wondering if there was a reason this function doesn't make that same assumption?

messages.subject: Re: HTML Page Network D3 Output Problem
messages.subject_clean: HTML Page Network D3 Output Problem
messages.body_plain:
networkD3 has JS/CSS dependencies that aren't being imported; they're automatically imported when you use ui.R to assemble your UI. We've just released a new version of htmltools (v0.3) that lets you write HTML templates but still define inputs, outputs, and htmlwidgets using R: ui.R ----- htmltools::htmlTemplate("template.html", force = simpleNetworkOutput("force") # or whatever ) template.html should be alongside ui.R (or you can put it anywhere else in the app dir and pass a relative path to htmlTemplate). Inside of template.html make it just like your index.html but don't include the CSS/JS references for Shiny at the top, instead in include {{ headContent() }}. And wherever you want that network output, say {{ force }}. We are still writing the docs for this feature, hopefully that's enough to get you started. messages.subject: Re: Observer class - details
messages.subject_clean: Observer class - details
messages.body_plain:
What do you think the return value of observeEvent(...) is supposed to represent? There's no "value" that you can get out of it--that object only exists so you can suspend/resume the observer from executing, or destroy it altogether.

It's more likely you want to do something like this:

dat <- reactiveValues(v1 = NULL, v2 = NULL)

observeEvent(input$button1, {
  dat$v1 <- ...
})
observeEvent(input$button2, {
  dat$v2 <- ...
})

Or better yet, forget the reactiveValues entirely and do:

r1 <- eventReactive(input$button1, {...})
r2 <- eventReactive(input$button2, {...})

and use r1() and r2() everywhere you were going to read dat$v1 and dat$v2.

If this doesn't make any sense, feel free to show more of your code and we can get concrete.

messages.subject: Re: Observer class - details
messages.subject_clean: Observer class - details
messages.body_plain:
Sounds like you're doing this:

dat$v2 <- eventReactive(...)

Don't do that. Instead do:

r2 <- eventReactive(...)

and then everywhere you want to read that value (like in renderTable) you call:

r2()

That "object of type 'closure' is not subsettable" usually means you forgot the (). Your example would probably work if you referred to dat$v2(), but there's really no reason at all to assign an event reactive to a reactive values object in this case.

And you never, never want to assign output$whatever inside an eventReactive block.

These are general rules that you should try hard to follow, I'll expand greatly on this in the new year:

0) Assigning things to output$xxx, writing things to disk, making a POST request, are examples of side effects. Reading from disk, calculating values, making a GET request, are not.
1) Anything with side effects should NEVER be done inside of reactive() or eventReactive(). reactive() and eventReactive() are used for calculating values, not performing actions.
2) Side effects that need to be performed reactively should always be done in observe() or observeEvent(). observe() and observeEvent() are always used for performing actions, as they don't return any values from the code that you put in them.
3) Assigning output$xxx <- renderXXX(...) should rarely be done inside of observe() or observeEvent(), and never in reactive() or eventReactive(). Generally they should be done directly within the Shiny Server function; anything dynamic about them (conditionals, etc.) should be performed *inside* the renderXXX(...). People sometimes mistakenly think of output$xxx <- renderXXX(...) as setting the output to a new value; that's not right. Instead, think of it as setting the recipe that is used to generate an xxx, and instructing Shiny to execute that recipe as often as is necessary.

This email doesn't do the topic justice but again, this is going to be a message I put a lot of effort into in early 2016. It'll be the subject of a tutorial at the Shiny conference which will be made available for download, and we'll have some kind of article or tutorial on it as well.
